doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

chapter: Dixieland and the college jazz scene
title: Why college bands played Dixieland rather than bebop
summary: Dixieland was most popular through the mid-fifties; bebop was unknown at Hamilton and too hard, so college bands played Dixieland.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

It’d be much less likely then for a college band formed by students to be playing what you’re describing rather than bebop. It would be unlikely for a college band at that time to get together to play bebop, is that what you’re kind of saying?
Well in the first place we couldn’t. I mean.

But at Hamilton we never heard of bebop. We were up there. We were up on that hill up there. Who knew from bebop? So number one, up until the late forties there really wasn’t a lot of awareness of bebop except in very, very, like people, kids who were living in New York City and could get to 52nd Street occasionally and hear it. So there was not that much awareness. In the second place, when you did hear it you heard Bird and Diz playing at those high tempos and playing these funny changes. I mean you just right away knew you couldn’t do it. So that most of these college bands were playing Dixieland because it was the same harmonic structure that you were learning in your music appreciation course from Bach.
Some of those songs that you guys would sing that had sort of the same structures.

Well it was all standard stuff, it was all 32-bar tunes, it was all that. And harmonic structure you could figure out pretty much the chord changes and the chord changes were all pretty simple. And you could learn to play well enough to do it. And so the consequence was that all over the Northeast you had these amateur college Dixieland bands. Everywhere. The Crimson Stompers at Harvard, Tigertown Five at Princeton, Eli’s Chosen Six at Yale. You had a band at Amherst, you had a band at Williams, you had Hamilton, Cornell, you know, everywhere you had these bands. And I know that there was a similar thing going on on the West Coast. What was going on in the south and the Midwest I don’t know. It could very well have been the same thing was happening at Vanderbilt, was happening at Tulane, I don’t know. Somebody would have to look into that. But I do know because a lot of the guys that — the cadre of musicians who were playing this kind of music my age around New York, most of these guys had played in some college band somewhere. So I know that, you know, what they were doing. And what happened at Hamilton was there was a Irishman named Jack Kelly and Jack was a trumpet player, a terrible trumpet player, and I had gone up to Hamilton without my trombone but I brought it back after Christmas holiday.
